edits.english: Abaye said to Rav Ḥisda’s interpreter: Ask Rav Ḥisda: What is the halakha with regard to a non-priest conveying the blood? Is the offering disqualified, like other sacrificial rites?
Abaye said to Rav Ḥisda’s interpreter: He asked Rav Ḥisda: What is the halakha with regard to a non-priest (one who is not a priest) conveying the blood? Is it disqualified, like other rites?

If a person disqualified from the priesthood conveyed the blood, whether at the beginning (where a priest conveyed it afterward) or at the end (where a priest conveyed it at the beginning), the offering is disqualified. This is in accordance with the conclusion of the sugya (Rambam, Sefer Avoda, Hilkhot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:27).

The Amora (in this restricted sense) is identical to the Meturgeman in Mishnaic language. The Meturgeman in the Sages’ lectures was usually a Sage (and sometimes even an important Sage) whose role was to translate the Sage’s words from Hebrew to Aramaic, and also to say them loudly (so sometimes there was more than one Meturgeman, if they needed to make it heard to many). Often, the Meturgeman would not only translate but also explain, for the Sage would state the main ideas, while the Meturgeman would elaborate and develop them. And for this reason, the Sages of the Talmud called themselves Amoraim, as they saw their role as a kind of interpreters in this sense for the Sages of the Mishna.
